name: Act of June 22, 1874 ratifying in general terms the Shoshone (Brunot) agreement of September 26, 1872 (Royce area 539)
nations: Eastern Shoshone Tribe of the Wind River Reservation (Shoshone of the 1868 treaty)
promises: The agreement of September 26, 1872 ceded to the United States the part of the Shoshone reservation set apart by the treaty of July 3, 1868 lying south of a line along the Little Popo Agie, the Popo Agie and its North Fork (Article I, as quoted by the Indian Claims Commission, finding 3).
The Shoshone kept the rest of the 1868 reservation, the present Wind River reservation (Royce).
As consideration for the 700,642 acres, the United States agreed to spend $5,000 a year for five years for the Shoshone and to pay Chief Washakie $500 a year for five years (Commission finding 3).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found the 700,642 acres ceded under this agreement were worth eighty cents an acre, $560,513.60, and that the $27,500 paid was an unconscionable consideration; it awarded the value less the amount paid.

breaches.quote: less than four cents per acre for lands worth twenty times that amount was shockingly low

landTaken: The Commission found the cession covered 700,642 acres (Docket 63, finding 3).
compensation: The Commission found the Shoshone received $27,500 ($25,000 spent for their use and $2,500 paid to Washakie) for land worth $560,513.60, and entered an interlocutory award of the value less the $27,500 paid (Docket 63, 1954). The final judgment was not re-read for this file.
today: The same cession and the same Commission finding are already recorded under cession-1872-09-26-sioux-wahpeton and cession-1872-09-26-shoshoni, and again under cession-1874-12-15-sioux-wahpeton (the formal ratifying Act). This is one taking, not four.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says Chief Washakie chose the Wind River Basin as its permanent homeland, and that later agreements ceding the South Pass and Big Horn Hot Springs regions, then allotment, left about 2.2 million of 4.4 million acres.

openQuestions: treaties.json error: this record names the "Sioux, Wahpeton" (scheduleTribes) and the Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate (presentDayTribes), but Royce area 539 in Wyoming is the Shoshone (Brunot) cession of September 26, 1872. presentDayTribes should be the Eastern Shoshone Tribe of the Wind River Reservation. Not edited.

Duplicate: this is the third of four queue entries for one cession (cession-1872-09-26-sioux-wahpeton, cession-1872-09-26-shoshoni, this record, cession-1874-12-15-sioux-wahpeton). All rest on the same Docket 63 finding; the map should not count them as four broken treaties. Jordan may want them merged.

Royce p. 874 lists this Act as Stat. L. XVIII, 166, "Ratifies agreement of Sept. 26, 1872"; p. 879 adds that the agreement "had already been ratified in general terms by act of Congress approved June 22, 1874". The statute text itself was not opened.
The Commission held it immaterial whether the land is valued at September 1872 or December 1874, since the parties agreed values did not change; it did not discuss the June 22, 1874 Act.

plain.promised: Congress approved, in general terms, an 1872 agreement in which the Shoshone gave up the southern 700,642 acres of their 1868 reservation for $5,000 a year for five years and a salary for Chief Washakie.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1954 that the $27,500 paid, under four cents an acre, was unconscionable for land worth $560,513.60.
plain.today: The Commission awarded the land's value less the $27,500 paid. This is the same cession recorded under three other entries.
